rv.q: The romantic “plot” ... is scoffably slight. Yet ... the show has secured its staying power. Compared with John Travolta and Olivia Newton-John, alas, the tingle-factor of pure chemistry is lacking. The evening succeeds because it abounds with infectious, unfaked delight.

Nonetheless, Nikolai Foster’s production is brightly entertaining and blasts out room-filling energy in its big dance numbers by choreographer Arlene Phillips, with tight formations of sharp, rhythmic 50s motifs.
Though the humour in this production – with the exception of the loveably loud Mary Moore as Jan – could be cranked up a notch or two, this is a good night out.
All of this Nikolai Foster’s revival serves up with skill.
Alas, the more-or-less original narrative meanders purposelessly among a dectet of caterwauling Pink Ladies and gurning Burger Palace Boys.
Ultimately, this is a thunderously good evening out.
In other words, it succeeds on its own terms and we can't ask for much more than that.
But then that’s the core issue with this production, which feels caught between sombre realism and full-throttle, sugar-rush escapism.

Set at the fictional Rydell High, GREASE — the perennial first crush, school musical — has previously enjoyed long runs at London theatres in the early 1970s (before the film’s release) and again in the early 1990s.
But as it is, this slow and dull production of Grease is very much not That I Want.
Grease The Musical is a safe bet for audiences looking for a truly feel-good show in the summer nights ahead.
If director Nikolai Foster isn't the man for subtlety or dramaturgy, he and choreographer Arlene Phillips do lay on knock out set pieces, courtesy of their untried but energetic cast.
Nikolai Foster’s Leicester Curve production of Grease is awful mostly because it conforms to every expectation.
